title: Iceland crown seen stabilising after drop-dealers.
text:
REYKJAVIK, March 12 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention and increased demand for fish fuelled by the mad cow disease scare in Europe will help the Icelandic crown stabilise in the next few weeks after months of decline, dealers said. 

 The crown has been on a downward path since early May last year on fears about its longer-term stability caused by the country's high dependence on fish exports and outflows for foreign loan repayments and swap closures. 

 The Iceland central bank intervened on four occasions in January and February in support of the falling currency. 

 At 1030 GMT on Monday the crown was at 121.8 points on the inverted trade-weighted currency index , which the central bank uses to set the currency's trading band. The band's lower limit, or weakest point is 125.36 and the upper limit at 104.66. The crown was trading around 108 at the beginning of May 2000. 

 "So far the central bank's measures have been successful and now we are even starting to experience a seasonal cash inflow, such as from fisheries," said Bjarni Kristjansson, foreign exchange dealer at National Bank of Iceland (Landsbanki). 

 Asked if rising fish exports were also a result of the European mad-cow disease scare, Kristjansson said: "This is definitely a factor." 

 Consumers across Europe have been increasing their consumption of fish in the wake of the mad cow crisis which has seen beef sales slump. Fish accounts for around 70 percent of Iceland's exports. 

 Traders said the currency could still lose some ground in the near term but should not breach its trading band. 

 "For now there is no reason to believe that the crown is in any danger. I would not be surprised if it continued to weaken a little bit but in the long run I don't believe that it will exceed the currency band limits," said Sigurgeir Jonsson, head of derivatives trading at investment bank Kaupthing. 

 RATE CUT SEEN 

 Traders said the central bank may boost market confidence in the crown by cutting interest rates. 

 "I would not be surprised if they were to lower the rates in the next few weeks," Jonsson said. 

 "By doing that they would send a certain signal into the market... they were determined to prevent an economic downswing. Were they to send this message we would have every reason to be optimistic," he said. 

 After several rises last year the central bank repo rate now stands at 11.4 percent. The central bank said last month that it was not yet time to loosen monetary policy, but that it would consider a cut if there was more evidence of an economic slowdown.

title: Iceland  cenbank  intervenes  anew as crown falls more.
text:
REYKJAVIK, Jan 25 (Reuters) - Iceland's central bank said on Thursday it intervened in the local foreign exchange market for the second day in a row, buying one billion Icelandic crowns ($11.51 million) to halt the crown's recent slide. 

 Iceland's inverted trade-weighted currency index rose further - meaning the crown weakened more - hitting a peak of 122.6 by 1330 GMT compared with a high of 122.58 on Wednesday. 

 At 1448 GMT, the index stood at 122.40. 

 The bank said in a statement on Wednesday it had sold about two billion crowns worth of dollars to prop up the local currency, which has fallen close to the 125.36 lower limit of a fluctuation band with a central rate of 115.01. 

 "Our foreign exchange reserves are large so we can stretch them for a fairly long time. All in all we are very prepared for further interventions," Birgir Isleifur Gunnarsson, one of the central bank's three governors, told Reuters on Thursday. 

 He said no decisions had been made about further intervention. 

 Analysts say fisheries-dependent Iceland's crown has fallen out of favour due to scant investor confidence in its longer-term stability. The crown has also been dented by currency outflows stemming from foreign loan repayments and currency swap closures. 

 Sigurgeir Jonsson, head of derivatives at Icelandic investment bank Kaupthing, said the central bank's actions were logical and in line with established policy. 

 "I believe that if the crown continues to weaken and the index starts getting dangerously close to the currency band limit, we will witness much stronger intervention than we have seen thus far," Jonsson said. "The central bank has been very determined to protect the limits.". 

 "Although the crown may weaken to some extent in the next few months I do believe that if the economy does not suddenly start to worsen the bank's measures will turn out to be satisfactory," Jonsson said. 

 "But if the economy does begin to drop, these interventions will not be enough," he said. 

 Gunnarsson said the central bank was keeping a close eye on the crown. 

 "I simply cannot say what will happen next as no decisions have been made... But I can say that we are not planning any actions whatsoever at this point," he said.

title: UPDATE 1-Iceland cenbank supports crown with dollar sales.
text:
(adds central bank and economist comments, background, updates rates) 

 REYKJAVIK, Jan 24 (Reuters) - Iceland's central bank intervened on the local currency market on Wednesday, selling dollars to support the crown which has been weakening recently towards its currency band limit. 

 The bank said in a brief statement it had sold about two billion crowns ($23.17 million) worth of dollars. 

 "We believed there was a good reason to demonstrate to the market that we are adamant in protecting the crown by making sure it will not exceed its currency band limits," Eirikur Gudnason, one of the bank's three governors, told Reuters. 

 "Yesterday the crown weakened considerably more than usual and therefore we decided to send this message to the market." 

 The crown hit a record low 122.58 on Wednesday on its inverse trade-weighted index , which is closely monitored by Icelandic banks and investors, after closing below 122.2 for the first time on Tuesday. 

 The intervention took the index back to 121.34, but it fell back to 122.10-15 in late trading, with the dollar at 86.25/35 crowns, off an 86.47 high and 85.32 low, after closing at 84.91 on Tuesday. 

 CLOSE TO THE LIMIT 

 The crown is now perilously close to its lower limit of 125.36 on the currency band, whose central rate is 115.01. 

 Gudnason said the central bank was keeping a close eye on the crown but had not yet decided on its next moves. 

 "I simply cannot answer what will happen next as nobody knows what is going to happen. The bank itself has made no decision whatsoever on what we will do next nor when we will do it," he said. 

 Islandsbanki-FBA economist Ingolfur Bender said the crown had been weakening slowly but steadily for some time for various reasons, especially the repayment of foreign loans and closure of currency swaps. 

 "However, the most significant reason is that investors in general have little faith in the crown being able to maintain steadiness. Therefore, while the outflow in the currency market is considerable, the inflow is very low," he said. 

 Wednesday's further weakening in the crown showed the bank's intervention had not sufficed to stop the decline, he said. 

 The crown is now close to its currency band limits which the bank is obliged to defend, so a further weakening would provoke renewed intervention, he said. 

 Other options would be for the bank to change the currency band limits, move the central rate, or let the currency float, he said. 

 The crown has been weakening since the end of April, but in the last few days the rate of decline has increased. 

 In July the central bank was forced to intervene heavily and even suspend currency market trading after the crown fell through 112 on the index. 

 The bank widened the currency band limits to plus or minus nine percent in February last year from plus or minus six percent to give the crown, which was strengthening at the time, more scope to appreciate to counter inflation.

title: UPDATE 2- Iceland  c.bank  intervenes  to steady crown.
text:
REYKJAVIK, July 14 (Reuters) - Iceland's central bank intervened heavily on Friday to support the crown as the beleagured currency, hit by inflation worries, sank to its lowest level since late 1996. 

 The intervention, for the third day running, succeeded in lifting the crown from its lows, but the crown remained under pressure, prompting many in the market to forecast the central bank would resort to a stiff rise in interest rates. 

 Others said the government could be forced to act, for instance by cutting public spending. 

 But the central bank could take heart from signs that some players were moving back into the market to buy crowns. 

Central Bank Governor Birgir Isleifur Gunnarsson told Iceland state radio that the central bank had bought $38 million of crowns during the morning. 

 That followed intervention totalling some $50 million on Wednesday and Thursday, according to dealers. 

 Gunnarsson declined to comment on whether the central bank would hike rates to support the crown. 

 "No decision has been made about raising interest rates," he said. 

 The central bank is due to release the terms of its weekly repo operation at 1600 GMT, which would be one opportunity for it to announce a rate increase. 

 At 1410 the crown was trading at 79.73 bid per dollar, down from 79.12 at Thursday's close but off an earlier low of 80.62. 

 On its inverse trade-weighted index , followed closely by Icelandic banks and investors, it was about 114.90, down from Thursday's closing 114.19, after earlier going below 116 for the first time in nearly four years. 

 CROWN BUYERS RETURN 

 Landsbanki Islands hf (National Bank of Iceland) dealer Matthias Eynarsson said the market had been a one-way street in the last few days as the crown slid. 

 "Now market participants are returning who are willing to take a position in crowns, and that is creating the possibility for buyers and sellers to come together again in the market," he said. 

 The slide in the crown has been prompted by worries about inflation in the booming economy. The immediate crisis was prompted by a decline in the crown triggering stop-loss orders by corporates hedging foreign-currency borrowings. 

 Dealers said small investors were continuing to close short currency positions on Friday, forcing the crown lower. 

 Bunadarbanki Islands hf (Agricultural Bank of Iceland) said in its daily newsletter that intervention to support the crown over the past two days had totalled some four billion crowns ($50.15 million). 

 "These are considerable amounts in the light of the effect on the market, although the crown might have weakened even more in the last couple of days had the central bank not intervened," it said. 

 "An interest hike of up to 100 points can be expected in the near future." 

 The central bank last raised its repo rate in June, to 10.6 percent from 10.1 percent, taking the cumulative rise in the rate to 3.4 percentage points in about two years.

title: Iceland crown weakens further, rate rise seen.
text:
